newsitem.title: PERU: Peru crisis begins 71st day amid talks lull.
newsitem.headline: Peru crisis begins 71st day amid talks lull.

text.p: Seventy-two hostages held by Marxist guerrillas in Peru on Wednesday began their 71st day in captivity amid a lull in face-to-face talks between rebels and the government aimed at bloodlessly securing their freedom.
Rebels of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) on Tuesday wrapped up a sixth round of preliminary talks with government negotiators and agreed to meet for a seventh time on Thursday.

As with prior talks, no details of Tuesday's discussions to end the 2 1/2-month siege at the Japanese ambassador's Lima mansion emerged, but Peruvian officials were upbeat that talks were progressing.

"We are optimistic because, since the direct intervention of the MRTA chief, we are in more direct conversations," Congress President Victor Joy Way, a pro-government lawmaker who is close to President Alberto Fujimori, told local radio.

In Tokyo, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Wednesday told reporters: "As with the previous session, it seems to have been conducted in a very good atmosphere. They may be starting work to sort out points of agreement and differences."
Nonetheless, a source close to doctors attending captives said the mood of rebel leader Nestor Cerpa, who only joined in the talks last week, was darkening.
"Cerpa looks irritated. He doesn't speak with everyone any more," the source, who asked not to be named, told Reuters.
After Tuesday's three-hour meeting, Cerpa and rebel No. 2 Rolly Rojas were driven from a Red Cross safehouse where talks are held back across the street to the besieged residence.

"The talks have continued in the same atmosphere as the previous meetings," Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, representing the Vatican as one of three guarantors mediating in the crisis, told reporters in a statement.
The guarantors, who are sworn to secrecy, described earlier meetings as taking place "in a constructive atmosphere."

As talks to end Latin America's longest hostage siege drag on, word of the state of the hostages and their captors came from a source close to medical teams which regularly enter the residence to provide check-ups.

While Cerpa was increasingly morose, the hostages -- especially Japanese Ambassador Morihisa Aoki and Peruvian Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela -- were cheerful when the doctors entered the residence on last Thursday.

"There is an atmosphere of optimism inside the residence. Some of them play chess, card games, ludo, and others read books so as not to be bored as they wait for whatever is going to happen," said the source.
"Cerpa's attitude has changed in the past few days. Before the meetings he was very talkative, but now he only speaks with Ambassador Aoki and Tudela," the source said.
Hostages freed at the beginning of the crisis reported that the Tupac Amaru chief was courteous and approachable, even joining in round-table discussions on Peruvian politics.
While Cerpa now holds himself aloof from most of the hostages, his relationship with Aoki and Tudela has intensified since meetings with government negotiators began on Feb. 11.
"Every time a meeting is over, they (Cerpa, Aoki and Tudela) get together and talk," the source said.

The hostages were mostly in good health. But two need to have medicines brought in from the outside for serious illnesses. Congressman Gilberto Siura suffers from stomach cancer, and former Supreme Court president Moises Pantoja has a heart condition and severe arthritis.
The doctors also examine the rebels if they request it.

"Once, two of the MRTA women asked the doctors, half-joking but half-seriously, if they could do a scan to see if they were pregnant," the source said. "Anyway, they did the tests and they were negative."

The 15-odd heavily-armed guerrillas seized the residence during a cocktail party to celebrate the Japanese emperor's birthday on Dec. 17. Their chief demand is the freeing of 400 jailed comrades and their hostages include Fujimori's brother Pedro, the envoys of Japan and Bolivia, and two government ministers.
